utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. Good afternoon, everybody. All the accused are here. From the Defence teams I notice the absence of Mr. Ostojic and Mr. Bourgon. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer. General Smith is present already. Good afternoon to you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to proceed with Madam Fauveau's cross-examination and then we'll move to the next. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General. You were part in several military operations in several countries. Would you agree that in well-planned military operations to the greatest level of detail, even in this case it's hard to avoid having civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be hard to avoid civilian casualties. It's not necessarily the case, though, in all military operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember having a meeting with Mr. Akashi and General Janvier in June 1995?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least -- I had at least one meeting, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown Exhibit 5D497?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: It was a meeting in Split on the 9th of June 1995, and I'd like to show you page 3. May we see paragraph 12? In the last part of the paragraph, one can read that General Janvier said the following: [In English] What would be most acceptable to the Serbs would be to leave the enclaves. It is the more realistic approach and it makes sense from the military point of view. But it is impossible for the international community to accept. [Interpretation] What I'm interested in here is whether you were sharing this opinion. Did you think that the most realistic approach was for UNPROFOR to leave the enclaves and that it made sense militarily speaking.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I have time to read the whole of this document before I answer this? I want to refresh my memory of this particular --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, by all means, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could we go to the first page, then, please? And can we go down the page now, please? And to the next page? And on? Oh, that's quicker. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We've given the witness a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: My question was the following: Did you share the view that the most realistic approach was that UNPROFOR left the enclaves and that this approach made sense from a military point of view?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not sharing that view.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When Srebrenica fell, it was certain that the territory would be split between the Republika Srpska and the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, the territory of Srebrenica or the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I mean the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina but when Srebrenica fell, there were also ongoing negotiations about -- relating to splitting the territory?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were certainly ongoing negotiations. In one way or another they had been going on throughout the whole of this war, but there was no certainty as to where the split would be.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You mentioned the meeting you had with Mr. Carl Bildt in Belgrade on the 15th of July 1995, after the fall of Srebrenica. During that meeting with Mr. Bildt, did he mention to you a meeting he had a few days before but that was after the fall of Srebrenica, with the Minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Sacirbey?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He might have done. I don't recall it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to show you Exhibit 5D513. It's an excerpt from Mr. Carl Bildt's book where he described that meeting. Can we show page 3? I'd like to draw your attention to the paragraph -- well, that's on the right-hand side and that's the paragraph starting with the news that and in the middle of the paragraph it says the following: [In English] "I was meeting Foreign Minister Sacirbey in one of those charmless, half furnished rooms given to the members of the European Members of Parliament in the parliament of Strasbourg. Surprisingly, I was more upset by what had happened than he seemed to be. His calm reactions and controlled arguments still seemed me to be a mysterious piece of the Srebrenica puzzle. "Srebrenica, he said, had always been a problem for his government. They knew that the peace settlement would mean the loss of the enclave. So from this point of view what had happened made things easier." [Interpretation] I would like to ask you the following: You had many contacts with Bosnian authorities, and did you also have the feeling that losing Srebrenica made things easier for them?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, and I don't recall anyone raising anything -- saying anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to show you another document, it's a UN document. It's Exhibit 5D40. In fact, it's a document sent by Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan on the evening of the 11th of July, right after the fall of Srebrenica. As you can see, a copy of this document was sent to you as well for your information. I know that you arrived in Sarajevo not at that time but at a later stage, but when you arrived, did you have the opportunity to see this document?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would expect that I did read it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to go to page 2 of this document. It's the paragraph starting with B and then goes on UNHCR. And this paragraph, the following is said: [In English] "UNHCR reports that 80 per cent to 90 per cent of the population of Srebrenica total population is 40.000 people are displaced persons who fled fighting earlier in the war. Thus they do not have long standing ties to homes and property in the enclave and will probably be interested in leaving for Tuzla. An UNHCR local staff member in Srebrenica reported today that virtually everyone in the enclave wishes to leave." [Interpretation] So this paragraph confirms that the population of Srebrenica wanted to leave after the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it states, the UNHCR man is saying. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And then it further down, not the next sentence but the one after, the following is said: [In English] "Following consultation with the Bosnian government, and in order to avoid a continued humanitarian catastrophe, an agreement will be elicited from the Bosnian Serbs to allow all residents of Srebrenica including all men to leave for Tuzla if they so wish. The Dutch will be instructed to remain in the Srebrenica enclave at least until arrangements have been negotiated and finalised with Bosnian Serbs authority for the departure from the enclave of those people." [Interpretation] So we can deduct from this part that it was indeed the Bosnian government that initiated the departure of the population from Srebrenica with the help of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure who initiated the -- I mean, reading that document, it doesn't say that the Bosnian government initiated the idea. But according to that document, that's what they are doing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: From a strictly military point of view, can we say that the capture of Srebrenica by the Serbs was justified?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no military justification for a military act. It's -- the justification is in its political setting. So I don't think I can answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to rephrase it. First of all, can the witness be shown Exhibit 5D493? That's an excerpt from the NIOD report which refers to some of your declarations. Can the witness be shown page 2? So I'd like to draw your attention to the first sentence of this page where it says, [In English] "After the event too, it transpired that UNPROFOR had viewed the eastern enclaves as untenable. In an interview General Smith admitted that Srebrenica would fall sooner or later." [Interpretation] And then later on, there is a summary of your meeting with Mladic on the 7th of March 1995. Do you remember giving an interview where you said such things, that Srebrenica would fall sooner or later?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. And I would go back to what I have said before. Putting myself in Mladic's position, I could conceive of these actions and the reasons for doing them. And I think that's what I'm talking about when I'm being questioned for that report.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: It's quite possible, because looking at paragraph 2, the second sentence, the following sentence is said: [In English] "In early 1995, General Smith had told the US ambassador in Sarajevo, if I were Mladic I would take the enclaves."

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't think I did say take. I've used the word myself, squeeze, all along. Those were the words I was using when I was discussing my thesis.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you were in contact with the US ambassador while you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to show you a video recording from 1993, and given your position at the Ministry of Defence, I was wondering if maybe you could tell us a few words about this video. But before watching it, I would like to ask you the following question. When you worked for the Ministry of Defence, did you have information that UNPROFOR members carried members for --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Carried weapons, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: -- for Muslim fighters?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean supplied weapons to the Bosnians?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes, quite.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had no information of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a video that lasts approximately two minutes and 20 seconds. It's Exhibit 5D488.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, we are not receiving any sound. I don't know if it is accompanied --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, if there is a transcript, it's in Arabic and I was unable to understand it and besides, I'm mostly interested in the pictures more than the sound. I have two more videos where I have a transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one moment, yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm just wondering if we have any information about where this video came from other than the year, which we have been given, the location or anything else about the providence or location, anything, any details whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely. I received this video from the office of the Republika Srpska in charge of cooperation. The video was shot in 1993 in Zenica and I think I already said that it's a video from 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So this is a British vehicle, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a British flag on a white vehicle. I can't tell you any more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes. I fully accept that. Can we carry on watching it?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we can stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What we see on this video is that UN vehicles or at least vehicles having UN colours carried fighters that we called the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is there a question?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't interpret it like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Still, you said that when you were -- worked for the Ministry of Defence, you never heard of such things, but during your time in Bosnia, did you hear that UNPROFOR units were involved in such actions, i.e. supplying weapons or equipments or even fighters, all this for the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard allegations to that effect in -- when I was in command, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And did those allegations include the humanitarian convoys?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to show you the recording 5D518, and we have a transcript for that. I hope we'll be able to hear it. And in any case, I have a written transcript as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Has General Smith been given a copy of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm being told that there is no B/C/S sound for technical reasons, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Fine. But if there is going to be a question, I would imagine there will be, he needs to know what is supposedly stated in this video here. Take your time to read it, General, and then if it's necessary to watch the video clip, we do. If not, we can proceed with the question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "At the Ilidza checkpoint, the Serbian army discovered 24.500 bullets in United Nations trucks authorised to transport humanitarian aid to Muslims in Hrasnica. "A convoy transporting humanitarian aid from the airport to Butmir and Hrasnica was stopped today in Ilidza. Followinga routine check by Ilidza military police members, it was discovered that the containers with flour had a false bottom with steel boxes. This was good enough reason to question the regularity of the convoy. "Members of the French Battalion who were escorting the convoy were not able to tell us what was in the bunkers beneath the containers. "The convoy was held up, members of UNPROFOR, UNHCR, and the police were called in and in their presence the check was carried out. The containers were off-loaded from the trucks and with the help of crane the upper part of the containers were detached from the platform to which they were attached. Journalist: "Mr. Popadic, the check is now complete. Tell us what you have discovered in the trucks transporting humanitarian aid to Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPADIC
utterances.text: "Found in the trucks which left for Hrasnica this morning at 0945 hours were 5.000 rounds of 12.7 ammunition, and 19.540 rounds of 7.9 sniper ammunition. They were discovered, as you could see for yourself, in the false bottom under the containers. This is the second time that we have found aid for the Muslim forces side in weapons and ammunition in humanitarian aid in the zone of responsibility of the Ilidza Brigade. Journalist: "Did you see whose ammunition it is? Do you know? Where is it from?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPADIC
utterances.text: "All the ammunition was produced in the Konjic and was transported by air to Sarajevo airport and then by land. On this occasion it was being transported and escorted by the French forces and this quantity of ammunition was discovered. "We asked for the UN gentlemen for official information but we got none because, as they explained to us, they are not authorised to give information. "In an informal talk with the UNHCR representative, he claimed that they have nothing to do with the trucks or containers and that they were responsible exclusively for the load being transported in the containers and that they are not interested in what is under the containers. "The representatives of the Foreign Legion excused themselves by saying that they only escorted the convoy and the UN police claimed that they would examine the case and inform us of the results as soon as possible. "Right now we do not yet know who loaded the trucks at the airport and where the ammunition was loaded. We do not know what is happening with the checks at the airport and how many such convoys have gone past, but one thing is certain and that is that this is the umpteenth time that we see that UNPROFOR is transporting and distributing weapons and ammunition to the Muslims under the guise of humanitarian aid."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: General, I think I owe you an explanation about an event in Ilidza in 1994. This is what this clip is about so that was before you arrived in Bosnia. Here is my question: In 1995, while you were in Bosnia, Serbs usually or frequently said that the roads to Ilidza was being used to supply weapons to the Muslim troops by humanitarian convoys, that is by humanitarian organisations and UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure that you have understood that this is the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I see, I'm sorry, I thought that was a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I quite understand why. But it is a question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't recall that being said in the way you have just said it. There was a -- there was undoubtedly suspicion that other things than purely humanitarian aid could get on -- be put on vehicles and so forth. That was said to us on a number of occasions and not only about Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'd like now to show you another video clip. It is a clip related to an incident which took place at Rogatica, it was a check-point for Bosnia, in 1995, while you were serving in Bosnia. It is Exhibit 5D519. I have a transcription of this video clip, and I must warn you the sound in the B/C/S version is of very poor quality.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this video clip be shown, please?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Along with food for the people of the Muslim enclave of Zepa, the UNHCR representatives were transporting ammunition for Muslim soldiers. "At the Rogatica check-point, a routine inspection of the convoy loaded at the UNHCR warehouse in Pancevo turned up ammunition o various calibres hidden among the goods, mainly the flour, and in the cabs of the trucks. VRS soldier: "While inspecting the convoy, in about the fifth sack I checked using a knife, I noticed there was something in the flour. When I carried out a regular inspection, I discovered the ammunition. "Without a doubt this sort of conduct represents the severest form of criminal activity and is utterly in contradiction with the mandate and nature of humanitarian missions. "Whether or not they felt caught in the act by the ammunition found in the convoy the leader and one of the drivers reacted as follows: Convoy member: I do not know anything about the ammunition found in the flour and I have nothing to say. Convoy Member: "I don't know where the ammunition in the truck came from. I don't know what to say, I cannot say anything really. Commander of the Army of Republika Sprska, Colonel General Ratko Mladic, sent protests to the UNHCR offices in Sagreb, Belgrade and Pale, and asked that competent officials there take immediate measures to avoid similar incidents in the future. "General Mladic also informed the UNHCR representatives about the fate of the convoy that was stopped and its personnel. General Mladic's statement said that the goods will be confiscated and appropriate legal measures taken against those responsible. "What else can we say as we watch the images from Rogatica that best testify to the human nature of international humanitarian organisations? "Need we remind them that they have always been welcome and safe on the Serbian side in the former Bosnia and Herzegovina? Need we remind them that the food for the Muslim population arrives in these convoys above all because of the understanding of the Serbs? Need we remind them how many times this understanding has been abused? Should they ask themselves who has the right to transport ammunition and weapons along with food? "It seems they should. Pictures tell best and most eloquently on whose side the truth lies."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In this video, mention is made of a letter of protest sent by General Mladic to the UNHCR representatives. Did you have meetings with the UNHCR on allegations of supply of weapons to the Muslims by humanitarian convoys?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: When was this incident?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but when in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In April 1995?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: April 1995. I don't recall a meeting -- a specific meeting with UNHCR on this subject, and I remark that General Mladic is writing to the UNHCR elsewhere than Sarajevo. So I don't know where this convoy came from. It doesn't appear to have UNPROFOR with it at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This convoy came from Pancevo.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Remind me where that is. Could you remind me where that is?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This is in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it came from Serbia to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not very clear how it gets to Rogatica then.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I can't tell you, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems a rather long route. I don't recall this incident. And I'm working solely off this transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At any rate, my question was of a more general nature. While you were in Bosnia, did you have meetings with UNHCR representatives concerning the supply of weapons to Muslims?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I do not recall having a meeting about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When the Serbs were saying that UNPROFOR was involved, and I'm not talking about that specific incident but more generally involved in the supply of weapons to Muslims, did you investigate the matter?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I had a specific allegation, yes, we would investigate it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do we have reports that were drafted after the investigations you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would imagine so. I don't recall the -- what bureaucratic process took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Were you informed of the outcomes of such investigations?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I expect I was. Again, I would have -- I can't recall a specific case.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you agree that the transport of weapons and equipment -- such equipment in humanitarian convoys is forbidden?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't what we were supposed to be doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And in a particular armed conflict, when one party clears convoys through its territory so that humanitarian aid can reach the population of the other party, the authorising party is entitled to check whether or not such convoys do not carry forbidden equipment?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- indeed, that was what was agreed and done.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to the statement you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor in August 1996. It is Exhibit 6D180. While this statement is being displayed on the screen, I have one preliminary question. Is it true that -- or do you remember that in this statement, you described a contact you'd had with various representatives of the military and political authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I need to look at the piece of paper to see whether it's true but...

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown page 2 of his statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'd like to draw your attention to the last paragraph in the English version, or the next-to-last paragraph, to be more specific. You referred to the contacts you'd had with President Izetbegovic and in this paragraph, in the middle of the paragraph, indicates that you met him quite frequently.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'hm, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Take a look at the next paragraph, you're talking about your meetings with Vice-president Ganic. The last line of there paragraph indicates that you met him regularly and sometimes even three times a week. It's the last line on this page.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And I guess that you're talking here of the period up to the accident suffered by Vice-president Ganic which took place at the end of June. Could we now move to the next page, please? In the next paragraph, you talking about your contacts with Mr. Silajdzic, and at the very bottom of the page -- could we display the very bottom of that page, please? You mention contacts with the Bosnian military authorities, with General Rasim Delic, General Hajrulahovic, General Dudakovic. Now, I'd like to show you the third paragraph on that same page, please. You're talking about the contacts you had at the time with Minister Muratovic, and in the third line of that same paragraph, you indicate that you met with Muratovic more often than with any other Bosnian government official.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: If you were meeting Mr. Ganic three times a week, how many times a week did you meet with Mr. Muratovic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember to that amount of detail. There would be occasions when it might be at least three times a week but probably not, when I was meeting Ganic at that rate.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could we move to the next page, please? In the middle paragraph, the third paragraph, you're talking about your contacts with Radovan Karadzic, and somewhere in the middle of the paragraph, you indicate that you had no meetings with him after the hostage crisis in May and June other than a brief encounter in December which was the last time you saw him. Could you confirm that you never met Karadzic after the hostage crisis in May and June 1995?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's right except for that last meeting in December, is it? Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Then you talk about your contacts with Momcilo Krajisnik, and I don't know how often you met Momcilo Krajisnik. Could you please tell us how often you met him? How many times did you have meetings with him?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you the precise amount of times, no. What does it say in that paragraph? I might be able to help you more if I could read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the witness the last paragraph, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I can't remember any great number of meetings after that period of April-May, but I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the next page to the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: First we're talking about Nikola Koljevic and Aleks Buha. If you want I'll give you time to read both paragraphs. I'd like you to tell me how many times you had the opportunity to meet these two people. I'm not asking for a specific answer but an approximate number.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have thought that Koljevic was much the same amount of times as I did Krajisnik, and I'm trying to remember how many times I saw Buha, but I do remember him at the end in that paragraph but I can't recall, certainly not a higher incidence than Professor Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The last person referred to here, and I'm talking here about politicians, is Mr. Zametica and here I believe this is clear enough since you said [In English] The company of Karadzic with the exception of when I met him in the company of Koljevic. [Interpretation] In the case versus Slobodan Milosevic, on the 9th of October 2003, page 27364 of the transcript, you said that you'd met General Mladic some ten times in total. Is that an accurate figure, more or less?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll -- as long as we keep it at "some." We'll live with ten, yes. I would have to go back and find the diary and all the rest of it to be any more precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you agree that your contacts with the Bosnian authorities were more frequent and regular than your contacts with the representatives of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Don't you think that such a difference in the contacts you had with one party and the other could lead the Serbs to think that you and UNPROFOR were partial and pro-Muslims?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think it at all. We often asked to go and talk to Serb officials and were denied, and there was just as much opportunity to talk to us if people had wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: A moment ago, when I mentioned your meetings with President Karadzic, I spoke about the hostage crisis. Is it true that those hostages were free during the first half of the month of June?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think they were all freed by the end of, certainly by the end of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But they were not freed on the same day, all of them, I mean?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were freed in a series. Again, I'd have to go and look at bits of paper to give you any detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci, Madam. Who is next? Who is going next? Have you come to an agreement between you? I see you hesitating, Mr. Josse. I don't know. Usually we expect you to tell us --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'm clearly going to be the longest, and I suspect by far the longest of those who are yet to cross-examine this gentleman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before I ask to you proceed with your cross-examination, can we have a review of the time you require. The Popovic Defence team had asked for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We will not cross-examine this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's -- the Nikolic, I think yesterday you sent a message that you will not be cross-examining the witness. Do you confirm that, Madam Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci, Madam. Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour from what I've heard so far, I don't believe I'll have any cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Meek. Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It is unlikely that we will cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Similar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And Mr. Josse, you were unsure whether it would be four hours or six hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm still unsure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's start then. You seem to be the only one left.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I've got no option. It's clearly now or never, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sir Rupert, my name is David Josse and along with Dragan Krgovic, I represent General Gvero. Actually, the very first subject that I want to ask you about was the matter you literally alluded to in the last answer you gave to Madam Fauveau and that relates to notes that you have of the events that you have been describing. You mentioned a moment ago as well a diary. What diary is that, please?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not talking of a diary. I was talking about diaries such as would be available perhaps in some record or other of what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At the time of these events, in other words when you were UNPROFOR commander, did you keep any sort of personal diary?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an agenda, as what I was doing on tomorrow or the next day, do you mean? Or as a record of my thoughts?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I meant more the latter but --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't keep the latter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a -- there was undoubtedly a pocket book of some description somewhere in which I said to myself, I must ring my wife tomorrow or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Cmeric is a lady, who you just saw indicating to me, has the advantage over both of us. She understands both English and B/C/S and she is indicating to me that I am going far too fast because of course everything that I say and you say needs to be translated into two other languages. It's primarily my fault, and I will try and go much more slowly.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: So will I.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you produced your witness statement in August of 1996, we see on the front cover that Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter was present. Now I appreciate that this was a long time ago, but to what extent did he assist you in writing that statement?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: My memory as I dictated it, and would occasionally ask him about a particular event before putting, you know, dictating that bit of it. I can't -- I think that's what I did. I'm not entirely sure. And then presumably there was a draft which I then corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You and he, I assume, had parted by then. That is, you were both in different jobs which were not connected to one another. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, my memory, and that might be helped if we saw the date on the top of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's the 14th of August of 1996.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time, we are definitely not in the same jobs. I'm not entirely sure what he was doing then. So if we are both together, he's come out to my headquarters in Northern Ireland.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And in fact in due course, he was promoted to full colonel and then became a brigadier; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. We have been informed, in what are called the proofing notes that Mr. Thayer provided to us, that the following -- and I'll read it out if I may. "At the time of his interviews with OTP in 1996, and later with NIOD, he had some documents which he had retained from his time as commander UNPROFOR. The documents were ones which had gone out under his signature and also consisted of Baxter's notes of meetings at which he was present. "He does not recall giving copies of these documents to the OTP; although, he did refer to them during the interview and the witness statement clearly refers to them. He believes he gave copies of the documents to NIOD. He destroyed the documents when he was at SHAPE" First of all, SHAPE is a NATO --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the anagram for the supreme headquarters allied powers you were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My second question is what documents are you referring to there, please?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I left the command, there were what you might call my personal files. They would contain -- it contained copies of those documents such as we've seen, the reports by Baxter and reports, those documents I drafted myself, such as that one we've seen again of the situation immediately after the fall of Srebrenica, when I've just got back into Sarajevo. They went with me when I left the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you can confirm that they were destroyed at some point in time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge they were all got rid of when I left the service in -- which, when I was at SHAPE.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now in preparation for the 1996 witness statement, you were clearly and understandably reliant on the fairly full memoranda from Baxter, many of which this Court has already seen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you came to prepare for the -- your evidence in the cases of Slobodan Milosevic, Dragomir Milosevic, and now in relation to these seven accused, did you have any other notes which you were or are able to refer to at all?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other than -- and I don't actually remember whether I did -- because if I remember correctly, I'm still serving when the Milosevic case is -- occurs, I'm -- I don't have anything other than those to refer to when they existed. I answered that, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And one or two other questions on this. Your book, "The Utility of Force," fairly extensive chapter on Bosnia, correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Primarily you deal with events in a chronological sequence. How did you gather the material together for that in order to recount your own personal tale and movements?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some of it's memory. Some of it's drawing on other accounts. I don't actually remember having any difficulty in going through the dates of -- and the general flow of that chapter, and if we were referring to anything, it was looking up things like the UN report on Srebrenica and so forth, which were -- gave us the details we required.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you as a matter of interest have Baxter's memoranda to hand?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think I did. They would have gone by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you can confirm that you do not have in your possession any personal note that relates to this time, of any detail? I'm not referring, let me hastily add to personal mementos or jottings of a few words, but I'm talking about significant --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not think I possess the documents such as we've been having shown here, tucked in some file somewhere we may find one or two, but I don't have a great sort of body of documents, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving on, if I can deal with this very briefly and it's fairly obvious, you are relating to us events that took place over 12 years ago, memory fades over a 12 year period; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You have understandably peppered your evidence with the words, "I think" and "to the best of my recollection" for obvious and sensible reasons. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The past 12 years have been busy years for you, some in services you've described, and when you retired from the British army, you continued to lead a busy and active professional life?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So much so, and I don't mean to embarrass you here, but by way of example you couldn't fit into your schedule an hour to see me prior to giving evidence in this case. That's an illustration of the sort of busy professional life you lead, sir, correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have another five minutes until the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I was going to move on to another --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think looking to your eyes I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think I can finish the next subject in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Next subject, Sir Rupert, relates to protocol and it's protocol of whom you dealt with and who dealt with whom when you were UNPROFOR commander. For the most part, your point of contact was Mladic? He being your fellow commander, correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A point of contact, I'm not sure is quite the word I'd use, but it was he I needed to convince, if you like. It was he who was going to make a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Bearing in mind that General Janvier was the force commander, and was your superior, you being the UNPROFOR commander, how did that work in relation to your and his, that is Janvier's dealings with Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- what happened after the bombing in May was that the dealings with General Mladic was taken over by General Janvier, but there was nothing before that that said that either one or other of us must be the person doing the dealing with Mladic. The division, if you like, of to who was doing this occurred after May and after the meeting in Belgrade, both of us were dealing with General Mladic, as I recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And lower down the chain, would you agree that there was quite strict protocol so that, for example, in sector Sarajevo, General Gobillard's direct counterpart was General Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as a general rule, that's how it worked. There was a matching of the hierarchies.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I think your Chief of Staff, General Nicolai's counterpart, was General Milovanovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If we looked at the organisational diagrams.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Communication within UNPROFOR, do you recall how you communicated with Janvier, English or French or through an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We communicated in English directly, him to me, me to him, but General Baxter spoke good French -- I beg your pardon, Colonel Baxter spoke good French. And so if there was any great difficulties, we could go back into French and check, and I can't remember his name but one of General Janvier's equivalents to Baxter had very good English so there was another check that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what about with Gobillard?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, in English, but there was Colonel Baxter again, and General Gobillard had an English speaker on his staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I can tell you his name. I think his name was Fortin, does that name mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It rings a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. We will have a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sir, a matter connected to protocol that I want to ask you about relates to mementoes and gifts that UNPROFOR senior officers gave to the generals of the warring parties. Was that something that you personally engaged in?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I did. I don't recall it. I remember being given a small token by President Karadzic when I left. I don't think I handed anything over myself. And I certainly didn't see General Mladic when I was leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And perhaps it's my fault. I was more interested in the exchange going the other way, that is UN senior officers giving mementoes or gifts, really mementoes is what I'm interested in, to the generals of the three warring parties. Did that happen as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it happened in my case, and I can't recall of a case where it was done by others in my time, that I was aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I appreciate that being in the middle, as you undoubtedly were, of a war is not the same as being in a war oneself. However, I'm curious as to whether this type of gesture is or was something that UN generals were encouraged to partake in in order to try and smooth the waters with the generals who were actually fighting the war?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there was any encouragement to do it. No one was being urged to do it. And as I say, I can't actually think of a case where I knew it was happening, and I don't think I did it. I certainly don't remember doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you didn't do it for what reason? Because you rather than me putting words in your mouth, you tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The idea didn't -- I don't think it occurred to me to do it, and I -- I don't recall having the -- what sort of gift are we talking about? This is a question I've asked to myself. Are we talking about the sort of regimental plaque that one might have had as some token?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, sorry to interrupt, that's exactly what I had this mind?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then maybe that would be the sort of currency of that sort of thing, and you might pass one of those over, yes. But I don't think I did, and if I did, it was part of the, if you like, ritual dance of these events rather than anything of any meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm now going to turn to the various meetings that you had with General Gvero, but perhaps before do I that, to put it into context, it's right, isn't it, that he is not mentioned at all in your book "Utility of Force"?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe that to be the case but we could go and check the index, if you wish, but I don't think I mentioned General Gvero, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's also right that his name did not crop up when you were giving evidence in the case of Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall using his name then either, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to begin, so that we are all clear, with the four meetings that you had with him for which minutes exist, and the first of these you have told us about occurred on the 20th of April at Pale and the minute is P2936. And I think we can go straight to the third page because we've already looked at the second page, where you told us, and I'll summarise this, that you were accompanied by Mr. Akashi, Karadzic, Koljevic, Krajisnik, and Gvero were present from the Bosnian Serb side. And we can --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I just -- I was accompanying Mr. Akashi. He was the Secretary-General's representative, not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Explain the significance of that, please?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is my, if you like, political superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I may come back to that in a moment when we look at the entry in relation to Sarajevo airport but before we do that, let's have a look at paragraph 9, where you deal with the issue of safety and resupply of UN personnel. Do you recall whether General Gvero had anyone to assist him at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to suggest that he had a man there called Marjanovic, I'm going to spell that, that's M-A-R-J-A-N-O-V-I-C, who was some sort of chief of technical services within the VRS. Do you recall anyone like that being there?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's a possibility; is that correct? You're not saying --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying he wasn't. I just don't recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. And again, in paragraph 9, we can see that Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter describes my client's explanation as rather inadequate. What I want to suggest is that General Gvero said that it was the belief of the Main Staff that there were sufficient fuel reserves and that we can see that that is minuted by General -- by Colonel Baxter, correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, the issue was taken up again after the meeting, as we can see from the remark, this line in private discussions continued, my word, with General Smith after the meeting. I know it's an awfully long time ago. Do you recall how long those private discussions after the meeting took?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would imagine we went and had a meal after this and that the most those discussions -- those -- took place by either before the meal or -- and/or during the meal at the absolute longest.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. It may be -- I'm going to suggest to you that there was no meal on this occasion because if we do go back a page to page 2 and paragraph 7 we can see that the minute tells us that, "Karadzic and Krajisnik left early on the pretext that they wished to go to church." So you didn't have a meal with either of them, did you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not unless they came back from church, no. I'm -- I was only surmising that there had been a meal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you were unlikely to have a meal with General Gvero alone in the absence of Karadzic and Krajisnik. Would you agree with that proposition?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I don't suppose we had it alone, but there had been lots of other people there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I think we are agreed that this discussion outside the confines of the meeting would not have taken place for very long?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you understandably asked my client how he knew about the fuel situation, and I suggest to you that what General Gvero said was that the VRS had carried out some research into how many consumers of fuel there were within the enclaves, some sort of technical analysis based on motor vehicles, electricity use, generators, factories, that sort of thing, does that ring a bell at all?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't, I don't even remember any more than the absolute outlines that we'd had -- he was there at the meeting and this matter came up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to go on putting my case and I think that we may find over the next hour or so that you won't recall a number of things I'm going to put to you. Could I suggest this, sir, Sir Rupert, that if you say I don't remember, the Trial Chamber will know that you don't remember and it's a possibility. If you say that what I'm suggesting to you is incorrect, you make that clear so that we have a distinction between I don't remember and no, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll follow that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Moving on, he then explained that the VRS technical services had also looked at the amount of fuel that was going into the enclaves, and they looked at these two figures and the result was that sufficient fuel was being allowed into the enclave at the relevant time. That's the conversation that I suggest took place outside the confines of the meeting. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have done and to a degree it's supported by the conclusion in that paragraph that he said that there was enough fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to briefly look at with you at the use by Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter of the word "inadequate." Madam Fauveau has asked you at some length about smuggling. You accept that smuggling went on, the extent to which is clearly a matter of debate, would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept that those incidents occurred. I don't accept that it went on in quite the way you're describing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's have a look, please, at 5D31. This, let me tell you, is a Muslim document, that is a document produced by the chief of the state security sector of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina dated the 12th of January of 1996, and it deals with a wide variety of allegations of crimes committed in the Srebrenica area. I would like to go in the English to page 10 and in the B/C/S -- we're finding the page. The bit in English that I want to draw your attention to reads as follows: "In September 1994, Oric took 2.000 litres of fuel from humanitarian aid of which he gave 600 litres to Zulfo Tursunovic while he kept 1400 litres at his home in Potocari."

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Page 6 of the B/C/S apparently. Any knowledge of that type of activity on the part of a man I'm sure you have heard of, Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of that, I did not know. That is a new piece of information to me. That he might have done such a thing was perfectly possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And of course, were he to do that, the result would be that there would be insufficient fuel -- the result might be that there was insufficient fuel for the other inhabitants of the enclave. That stands to reason, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we move now to 1D19? This is another Bosniak document. Though it's headed 23rd of February 1995, it's undoubtedly written in 1996. It's a review of the events in Srebrenica, the year before, by a Brigadier Jasarevic and it's sent to Rasim Delic. And page 3 of the English is the first part I'd like to draw to your attention, about two-thirds of the way down the page, and at page 4 in the B/C/S. It says, "The increasing mistrust felt by citizens of Srebrenica for the civilian and military leadership was encouraged by the unequal allocation and manipulation of goods provided by humanitarian aid. Naser Oric and municipal officials, Osman Sulic, Adnan Salilovic [phoen] and Hanj Fedic [phoen] were linked to this. There is information indicating that these men smuggled humanitarian aid, weapons, oil, et cetera, and that they collaborated with members of UNPROFOR and even with the aggressor in their smuggling activities." Now, bear in mind that this is what I would describe as an admission against interest because it's a Bosniak document, not a Serb document. That doesn't mean to say it's true, of course, but that is something to bear in mind. Could you comment on what I've just read out?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise the name Oric. I don't recognise the other three of that paragraph named in that paragraph. And you don't -- this doesn't surprise me as a -- a report after the event, as people start to find out what was actually happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you know about it at the time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know what that is saying there. That, that in every one of these situations, there were power struggles going on, that people were hoarding, manipulating the distribution of aid, is common to these circumstances, anywhere in the world, let alone here. So that's why I'm not surprised that this is found to be happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next document is a Serb document, shortly after the meeting that I'm asking you about. It's 6D72, please. It's a report from a Colonel Andric to the command of the 1st Birac Infantry Brigade dated the 12th of May of 1995. It's described -- I know you haven't yet got it on the screen, but it's described as an order to prevent smuggling of fuel by UNPROFOR, UNHCR, and other organisations. And it says, "We have received information that members of UNPROFOR, UNHCR, and other international organisations have been transporting fuel illegally to Muslims in the enclaves of Sarajevo, Gorazde, Zepa and Srebrenica. "They smuggle fuel in double or large tanks on combat and non-combat vehicles which they empty in the enclaves leaving just the quantity needed for their return journey from the enclaves to the territory of the FRY or the RS." And then there is an order as to how to prevent this smuggling taking place. Any knowledge, Sir Rupert, at the time, of smuggling using that particular method as particularised by Colonel Andric in this report?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of us doing that at all, and if I had, it would have been stopped. We were not, as far as I'm concerned, and I'm speaking for UNPROFOR, smuggling fuel into those enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My concern of course is the use by Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter of the word "inadequate" for Gvero's explanation. The documents that I've just presented put what he was saying into some sort of context. Would you say that's fair?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might have done, although I think what you've just been showing me is after the conversation we were having with General Gvero in the chronology of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, only --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak for the word inadequate. I can't remember sufficient of it, of the conversation, as to why he used that word. It seemed to be appropriate at the time, I suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not going to quibble about that but I'm attempting to put it into some sort of context, and I think you're broadly speaking accepting that. But you're the witness, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept that on the basis of these documents, that would be a greater argument than the single word inadequate would cover, but I don't think those documents or anything like that argument was produced at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. I want to broaden this out briefly with one other document, which Your Honour has been disclosed very recently. That's not in itself a criticism but an observation and which hasn't yet been assigned a number. We have -- it's certainly not in e-court. We have a few hard copies of it. So perhaps if the usher could collect them. I'm told that the translation booths have all been provided with one of these, as has Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's restricted document that Mr. Akashi sent to Mr. Annan in New York, and it deals with the humanitarian situation in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's dated the 6th of July of 1995. And quite a wide-ranging analysis of humanitarian aid, and let me acknowledge that this is broadening the subject out to humanitarian aid in general rather than specifically fuel. You are welcome to read it; you particularly want to read paragraph 4, I suggest, and I would draw the Trial Chamber's attention to paragraph 4, which deals with the eastern enclaves. Whilst you're doing that, it has been sensibly suggested to me that I give the ERN number for the record. I'll do that now. It's R 0082030 through to R 0082035. And then at the back of this are some rather interesting tables. Not so much the one that's labelled "table 1" which is I think a projection of needs. More the second table, which is described as UNHCR food distribution to Bosnia-Herzegovina, distribution versus requirement, 93, 94, 95, and we can see that in January, February, March, and April, the percentage of requirement accomplished was actually fairly good.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I ask the usher to turn to that page on the ELMO so that at least the accused can follow my line of cross-examination? It's the penultimate page of the document, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would you agree with the question that I've just asked, Sir Rupert? I'll repeat it.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you would.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, we can see that January, February March and April of 1995, the percentage of requirement accomplished was actually fairly good.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think you need to be -- I mean, they are fairly good like then but they are not the requirement. And but this I think is applying to the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would these figures have been broken down into the various regions and in particular the eastern enclaves?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They might -- how does that -- I haven't seen the other tables because they mention different areas in the -- the reason is that the different areas are broken out in the main document. Yeah -- yes, if you -- I've got a third table on the back. It just says Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's right. And that's an important --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And there they are breaking it out by -- in more -- more finely, as it were, but it's only for the month of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that doesn't -- that's the follow on from that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. We can see in paragraph 4 that the text suggests that part of the difficulties in May was the fact that there were "The air strikes, UNHCR was forced to cancel some convoys to Gorazde for security reasons while others were denied access by the Bosnian Serbs." And that's understandable?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would you agree that that may have had a knock-on effect in June as well?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shortfalls had to be made up, if that's what you mean, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or do you mean subsequent convoys?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Subsequent convoys. What I really mean by that is would that have been an inhibiting --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I'm not going to take you through what the rest of that paragraph says. We can read it. It's of note, though, is it not, that about five lines down, it says, "Access to Srebrenica and Zepa was, however, unhindered." That's in May.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry I've lost the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Paragraph 4, about five or six lines down.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll repeat it. Access to Srebrenica --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry I was too far down the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- and Zepa was, however, unhindered?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So that's clearly significant when we consider this. If we could turn briefly to the first page, we see at the very bottom, internal distribution. Am I right it doesn't include you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why would that be?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is -- first of all, it's a superior headquarters. Secondly, he's reporting on UNHCR business, not mine, if you like. And the UNHCR was a separate, and from my point of view, supported organisation. I didn't run it. I wasn't in charge of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But you had responsibility, or a large say, explain to us please, in making sure that these conveys reached the destination they were intended for?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mandate, if that's the best word for it, was to protect humanitarian convoys and see that they got there, yes. But they -- I wasn't choosing what was carried in, the size of the convoy, or to whom it was to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And when they were run through Serbia, and out of Belgrade, I didn't necessarily have anything to do with them at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As I say I'm going to move back, if we can, to the document that these questions emanated from which was P2936. Could that be put back up on the -- in e-court, please, last page? I'm going to go to paragraph 10 on Sarajevo airport. This part of the discussion clearly took place before your private discussions with my client after the meeting, because it's apparent that Karadzic was present, and we see that the minute says that Krajisnik was upset that a particular pledge he had made had not been honoured, and then it says, "This issue provoked some heated discussion between Karadzic and General Gvero." As I recall, Mr. Thayer, in his examination-in-chief, asked you about that, and you said that you couldn't remember any details about that heated discussion. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: However, would you accept that it would be -- it was not a usual occurrence for a Lieutenant General, I'm talking about Gvero here, to engage in a heated discussion in front of the UNPROFOR commander, with the person who purported to be his supreme commander, namely Dr. Karadzic? A fairly startling event, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how startling it was. It was sufficiently of note that it's recorded as part of the meeting, but I don't remember -- as I said to you, I don't know that it was that remarkable or I might have remembered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's really what I want -- really what I was inquiring about. Were you aware, either then or subsequently, that very specifically Karadzic and Gvero had some significant and public disagreements at that particular point in time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it's not something that you became aware of subsequently from any briefing, anything you read, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any briefing or anything like that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Excuse me. The next meeting is the 25th of July in Han-Kram at the hotel Jela. It's 274 -- can't read my own handwriting, as usual -- 7. 2747. It's another minute from Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter. I'd like to begin at paragraph 1, if I may. This was -- no. -- A meeting as we see at the Jela restaurant, and it says General Mladic was accompanied by General Gvero. And it says, at paragraph 2, that Zepa dominated the meeting, Mladic arrived carrying an agreement, so on and so forth, and then it says, as you have also told us, that after two hours you and Mladic decided to move to Zepa. First thing I want to suggest to you is that Gvero and Mladic did not arrive at this meeting together. Gvero arrived there some time before Mladic. Any recollection of that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was -- I'm just trying to remember. Of those series of meetings, there was certainly one when Mladic arrived separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could easily have been that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't want to take unfair advantage because I'm going to suggest the same about the meeting on the 31st of July and indeed the minute confirms that for the 31st of July?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then I may be remembering the latter one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But I --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I have no -- if -- I don't remember them arriving neither together or separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And in fact I suggest that Gvero got there by car and Mladic got there by helicopter. But moving on, you asked my client, again understandably, whether Mladic was going to turn up, and he said, "Yes, but he," Gvero, "wasn't sure where Mladic was." Any recollection of that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Gvero went on to say that he hadn't spoken to Mladic directly. He had simply -- he, Gvero, had simply been told to come to this meeting with an interpreter. No recollection?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't, I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you give me a moment, please? In this regard, let's have a look, if we may, at P1339. This -- I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: A? B?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I want the English version. I'm afraid mine is not A -- very grateful, thank you. As always, Your Honour is ahead of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This is a very brief intercept and just stopping for a moment, you've been asked a little bit about intercepts. I'm sure you appreciate this, and I'm probably teaching my grandmother to suck eggs, here, Sir Rupert, but these are Bosniak intercepts of VRS activity. I say that because there are a number that I'm going to turn to in the course of my cross-examination. And this is extremely short, and the original, which is on the right of this screen, is handwritten, and then in fact, C, I think, is a typed version of the B/C/S. But it's also an original document because it was typed up by the intercept operators after the event and from that, we know that this intercept occurred at -- on the 25th of July. Take that from me. I'll be corrected if I'm wrong by my learned friends. We see the time in the English, 10.44, and it's very simple someone says, "Where is Miletic?" Second person replies, "He went to see Gvero." And then the significant bit is, "Tell Gvero to be at the place where he is supposed to receive Smith at 11.30 with that girl."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I'm noticing that in the English version, you're correct, it says 10.44 but in the original, which we also have on the screen, it says 10.35.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Your Honour's beady eyes, Mr. Thayer may have -- I don't have an explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think if display 1339 C, which is the B/C/S original printout of the call, that is upon which the English translation of 1339 A is based.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm never sure whether these should be broadcast, Your Honour. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is no name of the person. I don't think we have a problem there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One -- yes. There is the location, however. There is the location. So no broadcast. I don't know if we have had broadcast already. But you will look into that, Madam registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: May I explain to the witness he may be rather bemused by this exchange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: General, very briefly, we've heard in this trial from quite a number of these operators. They are all protected witnesses, and so their identity mustn't be revealed to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And there was no broadcast of these documents, incidentally, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The point that I'm coming to is this seems to suggest that Gvero is being told to meet you at 11.30 with that girl, who may well be an interpreter I would venture to suggest, and though it doesn't indicate categorically that he's not with Mladic, that is the overwhelming likelihood?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.
