utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move back to where I was at. Could 2747 be put back into e-court, please? Whilst you were waiting for General Mladic, apart from offering you a drink, my client spoke to you about various things unrelated to matters at hand or the war, and he explained to you that he was familiar with the British political system and that he'd studied that as part of his thesis on comparative political systems. Any recollection of that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm afraid I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Apparently he discussed with you the role of the speaker in the House of Commons, the House of Lords, the Prime Minister, and then he discussed with you various political philosophers, including J.S. Mill, John Adams, Robert Owen, and Bertrand Russell. Does that ring any bell at all, sir?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No I'm afraid it doesn't. How long were we waiting for Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. No, I don't remember this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mladic then arrived, the discussion took place. What I suggest is significant is that Gvero did not take any part in the meeting in Zepa. In short, he did not come to Zepa. You've explained you went there by road, Mladic went by helicopter, Gvero did not go there, certainly at this juncture. Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next meeting I'd like to turn to, please, is on the 31st of July, the one at Mrkonjic Grad, which is 2947. We can see in paragraph 1 of this minute that this took place at the Balkana motel at 1200 hours and you, apparently your helicopter had apparently been engaged and damaged, and then the last two sentences at paragraph 1 say, "General Mladic arrived, allegedly from the front line, some 45 minutes late for the meeting. General Smith was met by General Gvero who remained throughout." So this clearly, A, indicates that Mladic was late, and, B, that Gvero and Mladic arrived there at separate times, correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to suggest to you that in that 45 or so minutes, one of the things that Gvero did was to point out to you, from the terrace of the motel, where his home was in the distance in Mrkonjic Grad. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: My memory of that 45 minutes, if 45 minutes it was, is quite different. I was extremely irritated. I had just had my helicopter engaged and shot down when I was flying on a controlled route.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And my memory of that was addressing myself to General Gvero and telling him if that happened again, I was going to get extremely exercised. I don't recall him telling me where he lived, but he might have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I suppose that in those circumstances, what Gvero might have done was to try to calm you down?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He might have done, yes. I don't recall other than venting my spleen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have any recollection of learning during the course of that meeting that Gvero was from Mrkonjic Grad?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, although I have a general memory that that was the case. Whether I remember it from that meeting or some other time, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And one of the things that he discussed with you, very specific matter, was the local custom which was to have scything competitions, hay scything competitions and that was a particular pass time of the inhabitants of that part of Bosnia. Does that jog your memory at all?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid it doesn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I could particularise what we suggest occurred during that time. He talked to you about the fact that there was an association of national traditional sports, he described these sports to you, and in fact he mentioned that his niece's husband, whom he named, was a particular local champion in the art of scything, does that help you at all?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid it doesn't. I had other things on my mind at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But again, what you're saying is it's a possibility?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I can't say it didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Excuse me. Do you recall whether Gvero had anyone supporting him so to speak prior to Mladic's arrival?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The picture in my mind of his -- of him on his own, but there were certainly one, if not two other officers there, when we had the meeting in addition to Mladic; one of which I recall as being the air defence commander at Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Does the name Savo Sokanovic mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's look at the minutes of this meeting, and paragraph 4, please, because that relates to General Gvero. We can see that discussion took place of the HV/HVO offensive and the humanitarian issues that flowed from that, and you made clear in your evidence-in-chief that the international community in general, and the Bosnian Serbs in particular, faced a huge refugee problem as a result of this, correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it appears that what Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter said was the gravity of this problem to the Serbs is quite evident, Mladic has appointed General Gvero to be responsible for managing the humanitarian and refugee problem. And that is obviously a reference to the problem caused by the flood of refugees from that part of Bosnia and Herzegovina or from the Krajinas. I don't want to get hung up on political entities for the purpose of this question, but from that area, correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's correct. This is the people going -- moving people -- the volumes of people moving, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And at paragraph 7, as we've already seen, the minutes say, "Zepa, little progress was made on the Zepa issue as the matter is clearly not high on Mladic's current agenda." Basically didn't feature in the meeting to any great extent, correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd next like to go to the meeting of the 25th of August but before I do that, let's look, if we may, briefly, at the meeting of the 22nd of August, which is P2949. I want to contrast the 22nd of August with the 25th of August, if I may. The 22nd of August meeting, General Gvero was not present at that meeting, correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And in paragraph 2, we can see the interesting description of the meeting by Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter where he says a fascinating meeting which lasted five hours and included a barbecue lunch in magnificent surroundings, this being a place called Borike near Zepa, correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And there is various descriptions of Mladic's appearance and his mood and what happened at that meeting, but you regarded that meeting as something of a success, and as a step in the right direction. Would that be fair, Sir Rupert?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And then, you met with Mladic again three days later on the 25th of August, that's P2950, when both Generals Gvero and Tolimir were present. I'll just wait whilst that is put into e-court. And in paragraph 2, the minute describes the meeting as, "A brief and business-like meeting." In other words, it was really rather different to the meeting of three days earlier where, as you've told us, Gvero wasn't present and you had this long leisurely lunch in the magnificent surroundings of Borike. Would that be a fair contrast?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean it was very different meetings. Not only just the time and place, but I don't think it was quite as, the contrast wasn't quite the one that one is long and leisurely, a great deal of business was done, particularly because Mladic at the previous meeting, Mladic had all his other commanders there, and they were as much involved in -- the barbecue and so forth was as much for Mladic and them, or rather Mladic with them, as with the people with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry, who did Mladic have with him on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other commanders, there. If you go back, you can see that there were other commanders at the Mladic -- at the meeting in Borike.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's 2949 again, please.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not his assistant commanders but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. The minute says the meeting was attended by two of the local BSA brigade Commanders, several of Mladic's staff officers who have responsibilities for the area, and one local Gorazde civil official.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Riley [phoen] who is mentioned, was the British Gorazde force commander, correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, we have seen minutes for three meetings where Gvero was, for want of a better expression, at Mladic's side. I want to suggest to you that when these meetings took place, Gvero said nothing or certainly nothing of any import at all. What do you say to that suggestion?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said little and was clearly in support of Mladic, who was the dominant member of the meeting, at least from the Bosnian Serb side, on all those occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And take this from me, certainly no suggestion of Gvero saying anything in any of the minutes produced by Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. This is Mladic's meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'm going to move on to a different but related topic, and this is the evidence that you gave at page 17556 of the transcript, that on -- the last time you left Zepa, you had an encounter with General Gvero. The first thing I would like to try and do in this regard is find out the date of this alleged meeting. Perhaps I could help you in this regard. In your witness statement which has been much referred to already, at page 19, I don't think it needs to be put into e-court for this purpose, you say the following: "In the course of the period 26 to 29 July, I visited the pocket three times and there met with Mladic twice." Does that mean, Sir Rupert, that your last visit was on the 29th of July?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. We -- I'd have to find some journal or whatever of my movements. I think I went on consecutive days, and if the first day I'm there is the 26th, then it's 27, 28 are the other two days, but I have no better reference than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't mind confessing that one of the reasons I was at pains to ask you about notes and diaries at the start of this cross-examination was for this very reason. You've just said, "I'd have to find some journal." What do you mean by that, please?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there may be or may have been some record of my movements kept in the headquarters. If we haven't got it, then it probably doesn't exist any more, if it existed at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've got one document that might help, certainly -- that I wish to bring to your attention, and that's 6D198. This is a document that this Trial Chamber has seen quite a lot of. This type of document, correction. I don't think it's specifically this document has been seen but this type document. And it's a report from David Harland to John Ryan and General Gobillard among others of events that day. The second page we can -- can't see, don't need to go to it, it says "Negotiations on Zepa, (11)," we have got it there, that's helpful, "update, at 8.00 a.m. this morning, Ed Joseph called from Zepa," and I only mention that to put it into some context. If we could then turn to the last page, please, top paragraph deals with events at 9.00 a.m., paragraph below that, the events at 10.00 a.m., and then the third paragraph down says at about 12 noon, I spoke with General Smith who said that he had just seen Muratovic and that the Sarajevo was still holding out for something other than complete surrender. If you saw Muratovic in Sarajevo at 12 noon on the 28th of July, could you have been in Zepa that day?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Explain how, please.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would have driven there. It would be late in the afternoon that I was there, if I drove that afternoon. I don't know, been there by 4.00, 4.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So it's possible but it doesn't jog your memory one way or the other, correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that doesn't help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you had this encounter with General Gvero, who precisely -- I know it's a long time ago but this is important --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- were you travelling with, please?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost certainly Colonel Baxter, Captain Bliss or Dibbs, who were my -- two of my interpreters, and my immediate protection detail headed by Warrant Officer Davidson.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you saw Gvero, what type of vehicle was he in?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The picture in my mind is of a saloon car, a black -- I can't -- I couldn't put a name, a type to it or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was that saloon car accompanied by any other vehicle or vehicles?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have you any idea who if anyone Gvero was travelling with?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Again, the picture in my mind is of him standing beside the vehicle near this check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we have -- I think it's P -- could I have a moment -- 2493 in e-court, please? I think the reason it's taking a moment is it's a map and maps take a little longer to load. Yes. Now, I'm going to ask the usher to give you a pen, Sir Rupert, and to mark, if you can, where on this map you say this encounter took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to zoom in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would help if I could see a bit more clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which part, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's up to the witness, Your Honour. I'm entirely in his hands.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Go to the centre and bring it out, zoom me in a little bit. Okay. Hold it there. I've got to try and remember how we -- how this worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can zoom further, zoom in further, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm just -- this is an exercise in memory of a map that I wasn't following because other people would drive me there. So I'm having -- can we now -- can we come out now, please? That will do. Yes. I have difficulty in doing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry, would it help if you were given a pen and you marked the direction from which were you coming or going or --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's as easy to say it. From memory we used to drive from south to north, having come in from -- on the road to Gorazde, we then went north, and at a point somewhere in the vicinity, I think, of the place marked Brezova Ravan, there was a check-point, not a -- not the Ukrainian check-point. This was a Bosnian Serb army check-point, where you turned off and actually entered, if you like, the Zepa area itself. And it was there that I met. But precisely where that is on that map, I couldn't tell you from memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And so it appeared that General Gvero was going in which direction?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Into the pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Does the --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I was coming out of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Does the expression "IKM" mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's not a trick question. It's the expression we use in this courtroom, I think from the B/C/S language, for forward command post?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you know where the forward command post for this Zepa operation was?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the -- some of the communication vehicles up on the hill near -- on our way in, in the vicinity of this check-point. You had to enter, I think you went through the check-point and then those vehicles -- some of those communications vehicles were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So you think it was in that area, do you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in that vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And that was based on your observation of these communication vehicles?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Returning specifically to the encounter, did you note it anywhere?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When was the first time you told any investigator or lawyer about this encounter?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I think it was when Mr. Thayer and I met the other day, and we were talking through what you would call it the proofing thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I said what I then told the Court when he asked the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: 22nd of October of this year?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Is there any -- it's right, isn't it, that in addition to your witness statement, you've been interviewed for various information reports in 2002 on two occasions, interviewed in relation to the Slobodan Milosevic case, which of course accept is a different albeit related matter, Dragomir Milosevic case likewise? Is there any reason why you haven't previously mentioned this to anyone associated with the investigation and prosecution of crimes attached to this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only suppose because we haven't -- I haven't been asked about, you know, going through the events of Zepa in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was there any reason you didn't mention it to Mr. Thayer in what is -- we've termed your expert statement which in fact amounted to a question and answer session with him in July of 2006?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't -- I can't say there was -- I didn't mention it. I don't know -- didn't occur to me perhaps. There is no reason for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I mean, you were asked in that interview about -- very specifically about my client's role within the VRS and to draw various conclusions about it, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And, indeed, when you were answering questions, whether they were of an expert time or not, that Mr. Thayer posed to you towards the end of his examination-in-chief, you chose this as a specific example of my client at work within the VRS, yet you didn't mention it to him at all in the July 2006 interview. Can you explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection of being told, after this encounter, of Gvero being in the pocket and what he was up to there at that time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Which UNPROFOR officers remained within the Zepa enclave after you left for the last time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be the Ukrainian commander, and I can't remember his name and --.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Dudnik, sir.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry, Dudnik was his name, yes.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I think there was civil affairs officers -- officer there but I'm -- I'm not sure it was still Ed Joseph or the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Bezrouchenko?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Ukrainian. Yes. Which of those I'm not sure, but I think we left the civil affairs man there as well, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like you to have a look at a video still, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Stop it there. Stop it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just bear with us, please. A few technical difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to get back to the video and particularly to the still where -- which Mr. Josse indicated. It went out of sight too quickly for me to take note of the notation of the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. It's on the operator's screen. I can see that here but that's no good to the Chamber or more particularly to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. We need to go back a couple of slides before that map.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There. Okay. I'm going to -- it's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you can proceed with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unless you are asking him about the kind of look he's giving to Mladic, in which case we would need to see that closer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No. I think that might be a bit risky, that line of cross-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I was going to ask you about the man sitting behind you, who was looking on rather intently in the discussion?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that snap where you've got, as we are looking at it, Baxter is on the left, I'm on the right, and there is a man sitting between us, there?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we've got the still now. Do you recognise that man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The man in the middle?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's, I would suggest to you, General Krstic. Does that name mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Who do you recall Krstic to be at that time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was one of the corps commanders if I recall correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. He was the commander of the Drina Corps at that time. He was the man who I would suggest to you was in charge of the operation, the military operation, at Zepa. Does that ring any bells?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been in his corps area, I think, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, he was involved in that and I think there is no dispute and you'd accept this, wouldn't you, that General Tolimir was in charge of the evacuation process?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw that, yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the evacuation process was finished on what day, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, but it's probably tied in with, I think I -- the evacuation was over, if that helps us find this date, which is why I was not -- I was leaving on that last of the three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Right. So at the point that you had this encounter with General Gvero, the evacuation was over. That's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to deal, if I may, with some evidence, for want of a better word, relating to Gvero's movements at that particular time. We know that he was in Mrkonjic Grad on the 31st of July, don't we, because you and he saw each other?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How far is Mrkonjic Grad from Zepa, please?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you without a map, long enough. You've -- for the Serbs you had to drive around the north so --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we have a look, please, at a document just before the break? That's 6D195. Mr. Meek very helpfully is suggesting that I should perhaps have identified that video clip with some precision, in fact I didn't identify it at all. I'm going to get some assistance in that regard now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's P2491, and though I didn't specify the point in the video, in terms of the time, I made it quite clear the image to which I had referred the witness to, so I think there is no further problem there. 46.24 minutes. Grateful to Ms. Cmeric.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The document that's on the screen, Sir Rupert, is basically a digest type news report from a Bosnian news agency called the VIP news report. It's the bottom of that first page that I'd like to ask you about, please. Take it from me, because we could look at the next page that makes this clear, this appears to be a digest of the 31st of July of 1995, and it says "BSA commander, General Ratko Mladic, arrived on Saturday in Drvar 20 kilometres north of Grahovo and continued organising the Serb defence in the region with the help of assistant chief of the General Staff General Milan Gvero and other aides."

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry I can't find that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Bottom left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got you. I'm sorry, okay. I'm there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So assuming this digest report to be correct, it would suggest that -- I'm going to help -- bearing that in mind, could we get into e-court 6D196, please? I think this will help clarify where I'm going. Yes. So this is a calendar that we have produced for July of 1995, and we can see that the 31st of July, which is when you had the meeting in Mrkonjic Grad and when this press report is dated, was a Monday. The press report that I have just read out refers to a Saturday, so assuming the press report to be correct, that would place Gvero in the Drvar region on the 29th of July. I accept that there are a number of assumptions in that question but the logic would be correct, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If all those assumptions are satisfied, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm next going to take to you a couple of intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It may be a convenient moment, Your Honour. I haven't finished with this topic. I've got a little way to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll have a 25-minute break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I asked for witness to remain out of court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, before you create trouble, we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis as from now for the rest of the sitting. Judge Kwon had to absent himself unexpectedly so that's it. Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Really, it's to try to assist with timing. Very briefly, the -- pursuant to the Chamber's request, the Defence counsel met last night to discuss future scheduling, 98 bis and so on and so forth. Most of us then had a meeting with Mr. McCloskey before the start of the sitting today, and one of the things that emerged from that is it would probably be desirable if the Chamber set aside a period of time tomorrow, certainly no more than half an hour, to air and debate these matters prior to the break. Now, of course that fits in to the next question is how long I'm going to be with this witness. Your Honour, I'm still not exactly sure. I find it very difficult to give a precise estimate. I'm certainly going to be most of tomorrow. But we will make every effort to try and finish him tomorrow prior to the second break. But if that's not possible, then clearly he will have to come back, if the Chamber is agreeable to have a short period for the scheduling matters during the last session tomorrow. I thought it worth mentioning now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's definite, Mr. Josse and the others, is that we need to finish with this witness tomorrow. That's priority number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I will be able to finish in the time that I have -- that I have at my disposal which is tomorrow. Of course, Mr. Thayer says at the moment he has a little bit of re-examination. If we don't get to the -- I understand the Chamber is making that the priority over the scheduling, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course if there will be time we will discuss the scheduling as well. Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yesterday I received the response of the Prosecution to my motion related to UNPROFOR documents, about 100 documents have been identified by the Prosecution and they are currently asking for Rule 70 authorisation from the United Nations before they disclose these documents to me. I have no idea what's inside these documents but, still, I would like to reserve the possibility for this witness to come back on the 23rd of November, if in the meantime we receive the documents and if it appears that he should be cross-examined on the basis of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. Thank you, Madam Fauveau. Let's bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just before I proceed with a few other documents, I should have asked you earlier, can you remember the time of day that this encounter with General Gvero took place?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was it --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was it light or was it dark?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was light but it was towards the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you recall what sort of time it got dark in Bosnia in July?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, quite late.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can you help, be more specific?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have said 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we have a look at 6D199? One other document before we get to the intercepts that I had promised. This is another one of Harland's reports dated the 29th of July also headed negotiations on Zepa, 13. Page 3, I think we can go straight to. Middle of the page, we see it says, "Ed," clearly referring to Ed Joseph, then spoke and repeated that General Tolimir had told General Gobillard that UNPROFOR could evacuate the men of Zepa directly if the Bosnians would accept an all for all prisoner exchange. This seems to suggest that Gobillard was in Zepa on the 29th of July.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you recall him going there after you had finally departed?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that he came after me but that was -- I don't remember him being there at the same time as me. So it is probable that he was after me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And this also confirms that as of the 29th of July, Tolimir was still active in the pocket, correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that report is about the 29th, the events on the 29th.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Take that from me.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. Could we look at P1376, please? P1374, please. It's 1374 A is the English, B is the B/C/S. Now, this, Sir Rupert, is an intercept dated the 29th of July, and we'll remember from the calendar we saw earlier that's the Saturday. It seems to have been intercepted at 2230 hours, so quite late on. It involves a man from London, apparently a corps captain, and a man called Rajko Banduka. Do you know who Rajko Banduka was?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He was an assistant to Mladic's just to help you. And in the middle of the page, we see that the man from London says, and this is in B/C/S, not in English, "Oh, thank God, may I speak to General Mladic or is he in the field?" Banduka, his assistant says, "He's in the field, Gvero is in the field too." And then if we look down a few lines, Banduka says, "Because he's there, where it's critical." Now, critical at that time was the Krajina, not Zepa, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- I wouldn't know if that's what they thought was critical.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well of course you wouldn't but I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my point of view, Zepa was still the most critical, but I could see that Mladic might think it was otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. And then if we look at P1376 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sorry for the intervention, that's 1376, just to prevent confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The intercept I've just shown?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I thought you called for intercept 1376.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's the next one, please. So, again, A, English, B, B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This involves various individuals. This man called Savo, you remember I asked you about Savo Sokanovic. I'm going to suggest he was one of the participants. He was Gvero's direct subordinate, but you've already told us you don't recall that. A man called Rajko, a man called Mico, and at some point Mladic was also involved. And it begins with a conversation between Rajko, who I would suggest is the same Rajko Banduka and significantly this is the 30th of July, it's a Sunday, and this again was in the evening at 2215. And about five or six lines down, Savo says, "All right. Our boss, yours and mine, is in the native town of my boss, now let's speak to me." And it goes on. And what I'm trying to suggest in this intercept is it would suggest that the boss he's referring to is General Gvero, who was in his native town, namely Mrkonjic Grad, where you saw him the following day. Can you comment on that at all?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It would have seemed to be saying that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, what I want to suggest to you, Sir Rupert, is that you are mistaken when you say that you saw Gvero at that check-point, as you left the pocket on the last time you were there. Is it a possibility that you are mistaken?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a very clear memory of this event. I would be easily persuaded it wasn't on the last day, it was on the middle day, certainly wasn't on the first day, but I have this memory of coming out of the pocket, going through that check-point, and seeing this car and meeting Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: For the avoidance of any doubt, the case I'm putting to you is it took place on Monday and Gvero was not there at that place at any time at all. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, I have this clear memory of such a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And are you in a position to comment at all as to first of all why this wasn't, to use Mr. Thayer's word, memorialised anywhere in the 12 years since you say this happened?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Largely because I don't -- nothing has triggered the memory and nothing -- there has been no reason for me to have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or declare it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And would you accept that you might be mistaken bearing in mind and - I'll be corrected if I'm wrong - there isn't a jot of supporting evidence for Gvero's presence in Zepa at any of those given days?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept that there is nothing but my word for it, yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And that there are in this case thousands, tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands of pieces of paperer, and not one of them suggest Gvero was there. I suggest to you that that is an indication that you are wrong, sir.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be an indication and that's for others to decide, but I can remember what I'm remembering.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to a completely different topic. You were asked by Mr. Thayer about information that you received from the pocket when you had taken command of UNPROFOR, and you dealt in some detail with the JCOs. Were there any intelligence sources that were able to relay information to you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: About Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: About Srebrenica, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: About Srebrenica. None that were available to me at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If -- I'm going to ask you some questions in a few moments of time. If for security or other operational reasons, you don't want to answer them, just say so and I will not press the point. Perhaps it's easiest though if I show you a document so you know what information I do have. Could we have 6D181 in e-court, please? This, Sir Rupert, was one of the information reports that I've alluded to earlier and indeed parts of it Madam Fauveau showed you in the course of her cross-examination. It's page 5 that I'm interested. And this is headed "SAS and the Truth of the Actual Situation on the Ground." "The SAS entered safe area after May, I think." Just stopping there, the SAS are British army special services, correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: "There were no SAS when I visited in March. Late April, early May, we get them in. I would have been involved in the process of sending them in to improve general communications and to provide the forward air controller capacity. This was a great help but a couple of men have limited coverage and not senior enough to be in the debate but it allowed me to check ground truth." Can you expand on that at all, please?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and if this is what you mean by intelligence, then, my answer was incorrect. I did do this thing. I put those people in there. If that's what you mean by intelligence, then I misunderstood. I thought you were referring to higher authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I was thinking at one point of asking a few more questions before showing you this, but I thought it only fair actually bearing in mind this may be an issue of sensitivity, albeit it was 12 years ago, that I show you the information that is in the public domain already.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. And I don't -- that you put your own patrols out isn't in my book, my understanding, intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not going to dispute that.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to be -- you to understand that those are the terms on which I was answering your question. Do you want me to say about what these -- what I wanted these to be doing, these people?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- what I wanted was to have a link that I could rely on in terms of its communication, and that came with those -- that unit, the JCOs. It gave me a direct link to that commanding officer. He knew that these people were there. It wasn't a secret from him. And the -- and that gave me a reliable link if I wanted to use it or he wanted to use it. It put the forward air controller, because that's what those people could do as well, that I could rely on in to the pocket. And as I've said, it gave me a way of double checking information to be sure that what I was hearing was tested against some other set of eyes and ears.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were the JCO and these SAS men one and the same?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. The JCOs came from the special SAS.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you recall when they left the enclave, Srbrenica, this is?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: My memory is they came out with Dutchbat on whatever the day was, 21st, I think it is, of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Briefly and simply, how did they communicate with you, directly, through a third party, through Baxter? That's really what I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see. No. They had their own commander, who was in my headquarters, and the communications went to that commander and then to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Bearing in mind their presence in the pocket, how was it that you, when you were on your leave, didn't learn more about what was going on?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- because I was getting my reports from my headquarters and not directly from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And why -- Mr. Baxter was clearly a very capable man. He was speaking to you on a daily basis, correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why was it that he wasn't getting this information from these JCOs and saying to you, "General, things have reached an absolute crisis point. It's not a very good idea you sitting on this island in Croatia."

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, that's what eventually it was decided. That's how I got called back.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And on that particular topic, you have said categorically in your evidence here that the decision after the Geneva meeting was made by Janvier and Akashi allowing you to go back on leave; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page of this document? At the top, five lines down, it says, "Akashi and I think Janvier were both there and I imagine I asked them both together if I was to return to duty in Sarajevo. I was told not to return to duty and went back on holiday." Your use there of the word "imagine" is rather different, I would suggest, to your evidence in this case where you were adamant that it was down to Janvier and Akashi. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the question that I'm answering. If I was asked, for example, did I ask them separately or together, I might have answered it that way. I don't know the -- exactly why that is reported that way. What I'm quite clear about is that at the time in Geneva I am -- there was a conversation that went on in which it was discussed whether or not I was coming off leave and the answer was to go back on leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This was an important decision, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In retrospect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I would concede that with hindsight, it was not just an important decision but the wrong decision. Are you trying to shift the blame to Messrs. Janvier and Akashi?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It was their call, not yours? That's your evidence?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I'm not quite clear what the blame is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll move on. The JCOs, as far as you were concerned, they were fairly and properly there as part of UNPROFOR's role in the safe area agreement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The VRS clearly didn't know that you had your own -- I was going to use the word "intelligence," but it doesn't really matter what word we use, your own source of information from British soldiers as to what was going on?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they did know. It wasn't something we could have easily hidden. They were in British army uniforms, and they must have been seen going in.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The -- I want to ask you briefly about the issue of information getting in and out of the enclave and Bosnian Serb concerns about it. Could we have a look, please -- you've mentioned it earlier -- at the UN report on these events, which is P528? And it's page 55 of this rather mammoth document that I would like you to have a look at. Could we scroll down, please? It's paragraph 238. And the first -- this is headed, "During the preparation of this report, only two sources were able to recall any possible signs of an imminent attack on Srebrenica and at that only in the days immediately preceding the offensive to come." The first of those I'm not going to ask you about. Three lines from the bottom, though, it reads as follows and I'll read this slowly: "In another instance, an international humanitarian worker, not based in Srebrenica, recalled having heard rumours sometime earlier, that the Serbs might be planning to shrink the pocket. He mentioned this to a colleague based in Srebrenica, adding that if he ever saw anything which might substantiate the rumours, he would send him a short coded message, 'Say hello to Ibrahim.'. "On 4 July, while escorting a humanitarian convoy, he saw what appeared to be military preparations from Karakaj, where he crossed into Bosnian-Serb-held territory from Serbia down to Bratunac. He saw some heavy weapons and tanks and near Bratunac, tank tracks. On the basis of that he contacted his colleague in Srebrenica that day, asking him to say hello to Ibrahim, the signal of concern was passed on to DutchBat." The Serbs, and I dare say the Bosniaks as well, had to contend, didn't they, General, with UN workers, humanitarian workers, acting in effect as spies for and against them. It was a fact of life?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not necessarily operating in support of for and against them. The UN worker might quite reasonably report to the UN what he saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But this was not that. He was clearly reporting this to a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Does it say that? I thought it said he was an international worker and he passed it to DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well he said it passed it to a colleague, perhaps I should say, so it would suggest that he passed it to a non-military person, a person who then passed it on to DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read that as being the colleague was one of his international workers in -- presumably in whichever organisation this man is in which it doesn't tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, be that as it may, would you accept the proposition in my question, that the parties had to accept as a fact of life that there were humanitarian workers who would in effect act as spies for and against them?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept that there were these people, if you like, a third party, between and amongst the other two parties. I don't accept that they necessarily acted as spies for and against them. They may well have been reporting information, and quite properly so, to their own people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to another issue. Would you accept that during your tenure as UNPROFOR commander, Mr. Akashi struck a more conciliatory tone than you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: From your point of view, rather than his, because of course you can't speak for him, why was that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: His business, his role, was -- and particularly as I understood he understood it -- was to negotiate, to set out, to bring a cease-fire, cease-fires about. I think he arranged in total over his time some 26 of them or were party to them. And I believe that's what he was setting out to do and that would involve always seeking to negotiate and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The same question in relation to the force commander, General Janvier. Would you accept that he struck a more conciliatory tone than you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part, I do, yes. In part, I accept that. It's for entirely different reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He, and we saw this in that document which had to be given to me in hard copy, it was about a meeting in Split in June, I think, he, as I understood him, saw our role in a way that we were peacekeepers in the old sense of the word, if I -- old, I don't mean old. In the previous sense of the word, in the experience of the -- if I can put it this way -- Cold War form of peacekeeping, where both parties agreed that you were needed there, that you stood in the middle and prevented them going back to fighting again, like in, say, Cyprus, on the green line.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And in terms of the specific effect of this, it's right, isn't it, that you didn't have any meetings with the VRS in June of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not at a senior level. And I don't think I had any.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we have a look at paragraph 197 of the same document, which is page 47? It says, "On the basis of interviews conducted during the preparation of this report, it has been confirmed that the force commander met with General Mladic on those three occasions in June 1995. The main purpose of the meetings was to maintain a channel of communication with the BSA because the UNPROFOR commander in Bosnia and Herzegovina had severed contact with General Mladic not wanting to be seen -- sorry, not wanting to be or be seen conducting business with those responsible for taking troops under his command hostage. The special representative of the Secretary-General had concurred with this line of approach and was aware on each occasion when the force commander went to meet General Mladic." That's a correct statement of fact, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What was your view of Janvier doing -- conducting these meetings with Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perfectly proper thing for him to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was he doing your dirty work for you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I think it's covered in that document of Split, but I hold and held the view that you shouldn't get yourself into a position where you're negotiating when the other chap's got the thing that you're negotiating about. You're on a very weak ground. And so I wasn't about to start getting into any discussions with General Mladic until my hostages were clear of him. Otherwise, I was at a disadvantage. The -- if my superior wished to carry out these negotiations, that was entirely within his remit and there were reasons that we needed to carry out some negotiations in order to get the aid convoys in. But I didn't think it was the right thing for me to be doing it, and said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you at the time, or do you with the benefit of hindsight, feel that at any stage, you personalised your dealings and battles, for want of a better word, with Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it's personal. You're seeking -- you're dealing with another man. It's personal like this courtroom is personal. If that's what you mean, then, yes, it was personal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, let's have a look at an extract from your book, please, at page 366. I need to get the number. 6D186. Page 366, please. Could we scroll down, please? And scroll up, please. In the middle of the page, we see it says, "The third set of targets were those intended to change Mladic's intentions by attacking his personal sense of control. Clearly, the combined effects of the first two categories of targets impacted on this too. All the bombing was aimed at undermining him as a commander, but I also sought to attack specifically his need to control. "An example of such a target was a military facility in the village where his parents were buried. It was attacked repeatedly in the knowledge that in Mladic's culture a failure to protect the bones of one's ancestors is something of a shameful dereliction of family duty. (Matching these attacks and to increase the pressure, we told the Bosniak prepares that Mladic could not look after his parents' remains.)" That's personal, isn't it, Sir Rupert?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I just said we are seeking to change another man's mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you were effectively at war with him, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this stage, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And to help the Trial Chamber, what stage was this?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are in September, after the London Conference decisions, and after the bombing in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you felt that the UN were entitled to bomb the graves of the VRS commander for what reason?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, the graves of his ancestors, I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't bombing that. I was bombing the military facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, explain what I've just read out, please?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the -- my understanding of it all was that the -- where his ancestors were buried was in the vicinity of that village and that's where this military facility was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You in the book were not much kinder to the civilian leadership of the Republika Srpska, I would suggest. Let's have a look at page 347. You're describing -- scroll down a little, please. No the other way. You're describing, the bottom of 346 which we don't need to look at, your first visit to Pale. You say, "on my side I had with me my military assistant Jim Baxter, the UN chief of civilian affairs, Enrique Aguilar my spokesman Gary Coward [phoen] And a couple of interpreters. Opposite us were the three Ks, Karadzic, Krajisnik, and Koljevic, classified in my head as the mad, the bad, and the looney, who were the political leaders of the Bosnian Serbs. And of course, Mladic with one of his chiefs of staff." Not a very "politique" thing to describe Mr. Krajisnik as bad or Mr. Koljevic as an looney, is it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't at the time. I said it was classified in my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But that was the attitude you took with you into these various meetings with these gentlemen. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my classification of them. I don't think it was my attitude towards them, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So your classification in your head did not affect your attitude, is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be my case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In passing, we also note that you describe Mladic as being there with one of his chiefs of staff, another error, correct? Technical error, but another error?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Technical error, yes. If I can sell enough books then I'll be able to correct it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I bought a couple of copies, you'll be pleased to hear.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: One last thing on this subject. It's back to P528 and could we go to page 97, paragraph 453, please? Now, put this into context whilst it's being got up on the screen. This is in a section called "Resumption of air and ground attacks." So again we are talking about September, when the air war resumed. Paragraph 453 says this: "Despite these statements, supporting a strong line and now conveying a much broader interpretation of resolution 836, the Secretariat took exception to a statement made at a press briefing by the UNPROFOR spokesman just before the air campaign resumed." 'The aim is to cripple the BSA war machine and render its military capabilities so devalued that General Mladic is forced to negotiate.' "The Secretariat indicated to UNPF that it had been 'frankly appalled' to read the UNPROFOR spokesman's statement and reminded the mission that the declared aims of the air operation were to ensure the safety and security of the safe areas, notably by forcing the withdrawal of BSA heavy weaponry from around Sarajevo. The Secretariat emphasised that the United Nations had no mandate from the Security Council to cripple the BSA war machine and would not obtain such a mandate if it sought it. "There was no immediate response from Sarajevo prompting a second message instructing UNPROFOR spokesman to curb their 'verbal blood lust.' UNPF replied that it hoped the Secretariat would support its objectives, the air and land operations in which it was then engaged." Sir Rupert, were you responsible for the verbal blood lust that your spokesmen so happily meted out to the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the commander I accept responsibility for my subordinates. I think though that the question the subordinate was answering, and this is after the resumption, yes, is -- he was describing the NATO action, and what you're showing is the point I raised earlier, I think yesterday, that you had this -- you had two organisations involved, one UN, the other NATO, each with a different political purpose or forum to answer to. And they came together in Sarajevo. And I think that's where that particular answer emanated from.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a little bit about that tomorrow, but is your evidence that the verbal blood lust was down to NATO and not UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. We said that. I can remember the fuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I think -- my memory is he was answering a question, as it was, as to what NATO was doing rather than the UN. It became -- I remember it enough to remember that it was a fuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That brings us to the end of the sitting. We'll resume tomorrow and that's in the morning at 9.00. Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
